issues.description: The problem statement and UML require a SealSaloon constructor that takes a String parameter (SealSaloon(String)) for the saloon name, but both the provided template usage and the solution implement/use a no-argument constructor (SealSaloon()). This mismatch will confuse students about the required constructor signature and where/if the saloon name should be stored.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the constructor requirement consistent across artifacts. Either (A) update the problem statement and UML to specify a no-argument constructor (SealSaloon()) if the saloon name is not needed, or (B) update the template and solution to implement SealSaloon(String name), store the name in a private field, and provide a getter for it. Ensure the README/Main examples and tests use the same constructor signature.

issues.description: The problem statement (and UML) specifies a SealSaloon constructor that accepts a String (SealSaloon(String)) for the saloon name, but the solution implements a no-argument constructor (public SealSaloon()) and the provided Main instantiation uses the no-arg form. This constructor-signature mismatch between the problem description and the code creates confusion: students are told to implement a constructor with a String parameter but the codebase and reference solution use a parameterless constructor.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the constructor requirement and implementation consistent. Either: (A) Change the solution and example usage to provide a String-taking constructor (e.g. public SealSaloon(String name) { this.orders = new Meal[]{}; /* store name if needed */ }) so it matches the problem/UML; or (B) Update the problem statement/UML to require a no-argument constructor (SealSaloon()) and remove the reference to a saloon-name parameter. Ensure Main and any examples match the chosen constructor signature.
